claim: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS) is caused by a deletion spanning a ~2.6 megabase region on the long arm of chromosome 22.
source: 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome (22q11.2DS) is caused by a deletion spanning a~2.6 megabase region on the long arm of chromosome 22.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as an established fact about the genetic basis of the syndrome.

claim: 22q11.2DS occurs in approximately 1:3000–4000 births.
source: It occurs in ~1:3000–4000 births and is associated with increased risk of neuropsychiatric conditions including intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and epileptic seizures. (Cunningham et al., 2018; Eaton et al., 2019; Moulding et al., 2020; Niarchou et al., 2014).
evidence: This prevalence rate is cited with supporting references.

claim: 22q11.2DS is associated with increased risk of intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and epileptic seizures.
source: It occurs in ~1:3000–4000 births and is associated with increased risk of neuropsychiatric conditions including intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and epileptic seizures. (Cunningham et al., 2018; Eaton et al., 2019; Moulding et al., 2020; Niarchou et al., 2014).
evidence: This association is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Up to 41% of adults with 22q11.2DS have psychotic disorders.
source: 22q11.2DS is also considered to be one of the largest biological risk factors for schizophrenia, with up to 41% of adults with 22q11.2DS having psychotic disorders (Karayiorgou et al., 1995; Monks et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This statistic is provided with supporting citations.

claim: 22q11.2DS is one of the largest biological risk factors for schizophrenia.
source: 22q11.2DS is also considered to be one of the largest biological risk factors for schizophrenia, with up to 41% of adults with 22q11.2DS having psychotic disorders (Karayiorgou et al., 1995; Monks et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Sleep EEG features spindle and slow-wave oscillations during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
source: The electroencephalogram (EEG) recorded during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep features spindle and slow-wave (SW) oscillations: highly conserved and non-invasively measurable signatures of neuronal network activity generated by corticothalamic circuits (Adamantidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact with a supporting citation.

claim: Spindle and slow-wave oscillations are generated by corticothalamic circuits.
source: The electroencephalogram (EEG) recorded during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep features spindle and slow-wave (SW) oscillations: highly conserved and non-invasively measurable signatures of neuronal network activity generated by corticothalamic circuits (Adamantidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Sleep EEG features are candidate biomarkers of brain dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: The properties and co-ordination of these oscillations are candidate biomarkers of brain dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders (Ferrarelli and Tononi, 2017; Gardner et al., 2014; Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Sleep EEG features are altered in schizophrenia, including first episode psychosis and first degree relatives.
source: Sleep EEG features are altered across many neurodevelopmental disorders, including schizophrenia, including first episode psychosis, as well as first degree relatives (Chouinard et al., 2004; Cohrs, 2008; Ferrarelli et al., 2007; Ferrarelli et al., 2010; Göder et al., 2014; Bartsch et al., 2019; Demanuele et al., 2017; Wamsley et al., 2012; Manoach and Stickgold, 2019; Castelnovo et al., 2018; Keshavan et al., 1998)
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Sleep EEG features are altered in ADHD.
source: ADHD (Cortese et al., 2009; Gorgoni et al., 2020; Lunsford-Avery et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Sleep EEG findings in ASD have been inconsistent.
source: ASD although findings have been inconsistent (Gorgoni et al., 2020; Lehoux et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Sleep EEG features are altered in rare genetic conditions including Down syndrome, Fragile-X syndrome and Angelman syndrome.
source: and a range of rare genetic conditions, including Down syndrome, Fragile-X syndrome and Angelman syndrome (Angriman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The majority of young people with 22q11.2DS have sleep problems, particularly insomnia and sleep fragmentation.
source: We have recently shown that the majority of young people with 22q11.2DS have sleep problems, particularly insomnia and sleep fragmentation, that associate with psychopathology (Moulding et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study with a citation.

claim: Sleep problems in 22q11.2DS associate with psychopathology.

claim: Participants with 22q11.2DS made fewer correct responses in the morning test session of the memory task (OR = 0.631 [0.45, 0.885], p=0.008).
